title: Building with One Hand, Holding a Weapon with the Other
summary: As the wall of Jerusalem rises, Sanballat and Tobiah mock the builders, and when mockery fails their allies plot an armed attack. Nehemiah prays, posts guards, and rallies the discouraged people, and the work goes on with half the men building and half standing guard, every worker armed and ready to gather at the sound of the trumpet.
story: Nehemiah, the Jewish cupbearer of the Persian king, has come to Jerusalem with royal permission to rebuild its broken walls (chapters 1 and 2), and chapter 3 has listed the families and guilds who took up the work section by section around the city. Now the opposition that was hinted at in 2:10 and 2:19 comes into the open. The chapter moves from words to threats of violence, and from outside pressure to discouragement inside the camp. It shows the rebuilding of Jerusalem after the exile as a work done under pressure, and it shows Nehemiah's characteristic way of leading: prayer and practical action held together. The wall reaches half its height here; its completion comes in chapter 6.
historical:
Nehemiah came to Jerusalem in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes I (2:1), about 445 BC, roughly ninety years after the first exiles returned under Cyrus's decree of 539/538 BC. Judah was a small province in the Persian satrapy Beyond the River, the lands west of the Euphrates. Its walls had lain in ruins since the Babylonians destroyed Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC, and an earlier attempt to rebuild them had been halted by the king's order after complaints from local officials (Ezra 4:7-23). A walled Jerusalem would change the balance of power in the region.

The opponents are real figures of the period. Sanballat is known outside the Bible: an Aramaic letter from the Jewish community at Elephantine in Egypt, written in 407 BC, mentions the sons of Sanballat, governor of Samaria, which fits his appearance here with the army of Samaria. Tobiah the Ammonite seems to have held some official position east of the Jordan and had close family ties with leading Jerusalem families (6:17-19; 13:4-5). The allies named in verse 7 surround Judah on every side: Samaria to the north, the Ammonites to the east, the Arabs to the south, and Ashdod, the old Philistine city, to the west.
cultural:
Ancient city walls were built of stone, rubble, and earth, and Jerusalem's had been burned and pulled down generations before. The builders were reusing stones from heaps of debris, which is what Sanballat mocks when he asks whether they can bring burnt stones back to life. Limestone that has been through fire becomes brittle and crumbles, so the taunt had a point, and Tobiah's joke that a fox could knock the wall over plays on the same fear. In an honor-and-shame culture, public ridicule before an army was a political weapon meant to break a people's will before any blow was struck.

The defense Nehemiah organizes follows the structure of Israelite society. He stations the men by families (verse 13) and calls them to fight for their brothers, sons, daughters, wives, and homes, so that each man guards what he loves. The shofar, a ram's-horn trumpet used both for worship and for war, served as the signal to gather. Many of the builders came from towns outside Jerusalem (chapter 3 lists men of Jericho, Tekoa, Gibeon, and others), which is why Nehemiah tells them to stay inside the city at night rather than travel home through territory where they could be ambushed.
literary: The chapter is Nehemiah's first-person memoir, one of the most personal kinds of writing in the Old Testament. It moves in two waves of opposition and response. First comes ridicule (verses 1-3), answered by prayer (4-5) and steady work (6). Then comes a conspiracy to attack (7-8), answered again by prayer and a guard (9), followed by despair inside the camp, voiced as a short lament in verse 10, and by rumors from nearby Jews (11-12), which Nehemiah answers with arrangements, a speech, and a promise that God will fight for them (13-23). The sudden prayer in verses 4-5, spoken straight to God in the middle of the story, is typical of the book (compare 5:19 and 6:9, 14), and the closing picture of men sleeping in their clothes with weapons in reach leaves the reader with the cost of the work.

outline.t: Sanballat and Tobiah ridicule the builders
Nehemiah's prayer, and the wall rises to half its height
A conspiracy to attack, answered by prayer and a guard
Exhaustion inside and rumors from outside
Nehemiah arms the families and calls them to remember the Lord
Working and watching: half build, half stand guard

doctrines.note: Nehemiah prays and acts in the same breath: “So we prayed to our God and posted a guard against them day and night” (verse 9). The chapter gives no support to the idea that trusting God means doing nothing, or that careful planning means not trusting God.
The enemies' plan fails because “God had frustrated it” (verse 15), and yet the builders still carry weapons. God's rule over events works through human watchfulness rather than replacing it.
Against fear Nehemiah sets one thing to remember: “the Lord, who is great and awesome” (verse 14). The courage he asks for comes from a right view of who God is, not from underestimating the enemy.

words.note: Melakhah, work. The word is used for ordinary labor and craftsmanship, and also for the skilled work on the tabernacle in Exodus. It runs through Nehemiah as a keyword for the rebuilding (verses 11, 15, 16, 17, 19, 21 here). The enemies' goal is to stop the work; the people's response is to return to it.

Zakar, to remember. In Hebrew, remembering is more than recalling a fact; it means bringing someone to mind in a way that shapes action. Nehemiah tells the frightened people to remember the Lord (verse 14), and throughout the book he asks God to remember him and his enemies. What a people remembers determines how they stand.

Lacham, to fight. The same verb describes the enemies' plan to fight against Jerusalem (verse 8), the families' call to fight for their brothers and homes (verse 14), and the promise “Our God will fight for us” (verse 20). That last line echoes Israel's older confession that the Lord fights for his people (Exodus 14:14; Deuteronomy 1:30).

Chomah, wall. A city wall meant security, identity, and dignity; a city without one was exposed and shamed (1:3). Rebuilding it marked Jerusalem as a living community again rather than a heap of ruins.

christ: The link to Christ here is thematic rather than predictive. Nehemiah is a leader who places himself among the workers, shares their danger, and does not change out of his clothes while they stand guard (verse 23). The Gospels show a greater servant-leader who does not stand at a distance from his people but enters their danger fully. The chapter's pairing of building and watching also finds an echo in the New Testament's picture of the church as a structure being built on Christ (Ephesians 2:19-22) by people who must also stay alert and stand firm (Ephesians 6:10-18). And Nehemiah's rallying cry that God will fight for them points to the confidence the New Testament places in Christ, who has already won the decisive battle over the powers opposed to God (Colossians 2:15).

hard.q: How can Nehemiah pray that his enemies' sin not be blotted out?
hard.a:
Verses 4-5 ask God to turn the enemies' scorn back on them and not to forgive their iniquity. To modern readers, and especially in light of Jesus' command to pray for enemies, this sounds harsh. Several things help put it in context. The prayer hands vengeance to God rather than taking it: Nehemiah does not attack Sanballat but keeps building and arms only for defense. His opponents were not merely personal rivals but were trying to stop the restoration of God's city, and he treats their contempt as an offense against God, since they “have provoked the builders” engaged in God's work. The prayer also echoes the imprecatory psalms and Jeremiah's prayers (for example Jeremiah 18:23), which voice a cry for justice to the only one who can rightly judge.

Christian readers differ on how far such prayers remain models for believers. Some see them as legitimate cries for justice that the church can still pray against persistent, unrepentant evil. Others see them as honest but pre-Christian responses that the gospel's call to love enemies now transforms. Most agree that the Bible records them without asking readers to copy their tone lightly, and that handing wrongs over to God is better than returning them.

questions: Nehemiah answered each new threat with both prayer and a practical step. Which of the two do you tend to neglect when you are under pressure?
The most dangerous discouragement in this chapter came from inside the camp (verse 10). What causes good work to stall among God's people, and how did Nehemiah respond to it?
Nehemiah called the people to fight for their families and homes. What does it look like to protect the people closest to you while still doing the larger work you have been given?
